chapter.name: From Barter to Money
chapter.blurb: The barter system and its problems, barter today, the functions of money, coins, paper money and digital money.

scope: Detailed working of UPI and net banking

concepts.name: The barter system
concepts.description: What barter is, how it works, and the commodities used before money.
concepts.idea: Barter is exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money.
concepts.rule: The barter system is a way of exchanging goods and services without using money and was the earliest form of exchange. For example, you may swap an extra eraser for a classmate's extra pencil. People used commodities such as cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth, cattle, seeds and others. Other odd forms included Rai stones of Yap Island, the Aztec Tajadero and red feather coils, the Tevau, of the Solomon Islands. Money is the common tool everybody accepts to make or receive payments. Today people use coins, notes and mobile phones.
concepts.example: Exchanging an extra eraser for an extra pencil is barter.

concepts.name: Problems of the barter system
concepts.description: Double coincidence of wants, lack of a common measure of value, divisibility, portability and durability.
concepts.idea: Barter is inconvenient because of five problems, which money helps to solve.
concepts.rule: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each person must have what the other wants. It has no common standard measure of value, so it is hard to decide in what proportion to exchange. Goods may not be divisible, for example you cannot exchange part of an ox for a sweater. Goods are hard to carry, the problem of portability, and to store, the problem of durability, since wheat may rot or be eaten by rats. Money makes these problems easier.
concepts.example: A farmer with an ox needs shoes, a sweater and medicines and faces all these difficulties.

concepts.name: Barter today: Junbeel Mela and everyday exchanges
concepts.description: Barter that still exists, the Junbeel Mela of Assam, book exchange and exchange of old clothes for utensils.
concepts.idea: Barter continues today in fairs and everyday practices.
concepts.rule: Although money replaced barter around the world, some barter systems remain. The Junbeel Mela is a three-day annual socio-cultural fair at Junbeel in Morigaon district of Assam. It begins with the Agni Puja, worship of fire. Since the 15th century chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities gathered to discuss political issues and keep friendly relations, and a fair grew. Bartering begins early with roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs and spices and handmade forest goods, exchanged with people from the plains for rice cakes and other foods. Vendors offer new utensils for old clothes. Book exchange clubs let friends swap books.
concepts.example: Households give old clothes to vendors in return for new utensils.

concepts.name: The functions of money
concepts.description: Money as a medium of exchange, a standard of deferred payment, a store of value and a common denomination.
concepts.idea: Money makes exchange easy, allows delayed payments, stores value and measures worth.
concepts.rule: As trade grew and distances lengthened a common medium of exchange was needed, so money came into existence. It is accepted as a means of payment for goods and services. Money is a standard of deferred payment, since payments can be made later. It is a store of value: the farmer can keep money instead of wheat and buy things later. It is a common denomination that measures the value of goods and services and allows comparing them by price. Money moves in a cycle: parents pay shopkeepers, who pay workers, who buy essentials.
concepts.example: If a book costs Rs 100 and you have Rs 50, deferred payment lets you pay the rest later.

concepts.name: Coins: the journey of money in India
concepts.description: The timeline of money, ancient coins, their metals and symbols, coins today and the rupee symbol.
concepts.idea: Coins were among the earliest forms of money, issued by rulers with symbols and later accepted widely.
concepts.rule: The timeline runs from barter about 6000 BCE, cowrie, metal coinage from about 600 BCE in iron, silver, gold and copper, official paper money in 1861, debit and credit cards from 1980 and UPI digital money in 2016. Rulers issued and controlled coins; coins of powerful rulers were accepted across kingdoms, which helped trade. Ancient coins of gold, silver, copper or their alloys were called karshapanas or panas and had symbols called rupas. Variants of pana survive in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam (panam) and Kannada (hana). Coins showed animals, trees, hills, kings and deities; Chalukya coins showed Varaha and a parasol, Chola coins a tiger. Roman coins found in Pudukkottai show trade. The rupee symbol was adopted in 2010, designed by Udaya Kumar; 1 anna was 1/16 of a rupee.
concepts.example: The rupee sign combines the Devanagari 'Ra' and Roman 'R' with two horizontal stripes.

concepts.name: Paper money, the RBI and digital money
concepts.description: The move to paper money, the role of the RBI, denominations and new forms such as UPI and QR codes.
concepts.idea: Paper currency is issued only by the RBI, and digital money now moves without notes or coins.
concepts.rule: As coins became hard to carry and store, paper money was adopted. It was first used in China and introduced in India in the late 18th century. Coins are used for smaller denominations and paper for higher ones. Today the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) controls the issue of currency and it is illegal for anyone else to issue it. Security features help prevent illegal printing. Digital money is intangible electronic money; methods include debit cards, credit cards, net banking and UPI, which transfer money directly between bank accounts. A QR code holds the receiver's bank details and lets customers pay by scanning.
concepts.example: Krishnappa's fruit cart has a QR code so customers can pay by phone.
